item.title: Propaq: A Python package for Heisenberg Propagation
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Rust-backed Python library Propaq matches monoprop and achieves up to ∼100× speedup over existing packages like pauli-prop, pyrauli, and PauliPropagation.jl at 109 terms. Natively supports arbitrary operator bases and hybrid Schrödinger-Heisenberg simulation.

Grade 0.463 · 3.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Hrishikesh Belagali, Ryan LaRose

Figure

Propagation wall time in seconds (main plot) and number of terms (inset) versus Trotter step count for TFIM (left) and Hubbard (right) models across multiple propagation packages using 64 threads and a 10−6 coefficient cutoff.

Asks

How to implement a flexible, high-performance Heisenberg propagation package supporting arbitrary operator bases and hybrid simulation schemes?

Before

Packages including pauli-prop, pyrauli, PauliPropagation.jl, and MajoranaPropagation.jl.

But

Coefficient truncation threshold of 10−6; benchmarks evaluated on 64 AMD EPYC 7H12 cores for Trotterized 2D TFIM and 2D Hubbard models.

Tools

Rust core with Python bindings · Heisenberg propagation (Pauli, Majorana, Weyl-Heisenberg) · Matrix product state Schrödinger simulation · Multi-threaded CPU parallelization

Abstract

We introduce Propaq, a performant and flexible Python package implementing Heisenberg propagation techniques for classically simulating quantum circuits. Propaq is compatible with major quantum software packages like Qiskit and Cirq, and matches or outperforms similar state-of-the-art packages for Heisenberg propagation. Beyond this, Propaq has multiple distinguishing features for simulation and research. These include Heisenberg propagation in any basis, hybrid Schrödinger-Heisenberg simulation, custom truncation and noisy simulation methods, and detailed logging information for analyzing simulation accuracy, runtime, and memory usage. We describe these features, how to use Propaq for research, and its backend implementation.

item.title: From NISQ to Fault-Tolerance: Applications and Algorithmic Benchmarks for Spin Qubits
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Compiling Parity Twine to exchange-only (EO) spin qubits reduces the physical exchange-pulse count by more than 22% for QFT and up to 34% for QAOA compared to baseline compilation schemes.

Grade 0.437 · 2.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Frederik Lohof, Florian Ginzel, Wolfgang Lechner

Figure

Physical exchange-pulse count and Twine/Fowler pulse count ratio as a function of device length L for the quantum Fourier transform.

Asks

How do algorithmic benchmarks and simulation routines scale from NISQ to fault-tolerance when mapped directly to physical exchange-pulse sequences on exchange-only spin qubit QPUs?

But

Analytical and numerical compilation models; assumes single-pulse error rates p≈1.5×10−4, readout error pm≈0.01, and T2≈19.3 μs.

Tools

Parity Twine compilation · exchange-only (EO) spin qubits · pulse-level scheduling with exclusion radius · surface code QEC / lattice surgery error modeling

Abstract

Motivated by recent breakthroughs in the development of spin-based quantum processing units based on exchange-only (EO) spin qubits, we provide a roadmap for the implementation of quantum algorithms on the EO platform, ranging from the NISQ to the fault-tolerant era. To provide an algorithm-driven perspective on the scaling of quantum chips, we consider a range of applications targeting different stages of hardware maturity and formulate requirements for a successful realization. We show that the compilation method Parity Twine perfectly complements the hardware's capabilities to perform tasks such as the quantum Fourier transform or QAOA. Furthermore, we describe an error detection technique native to Parity Twine, which EO qubits can leverage in a unique and advantageous way to improve algorithm performance. Finally, since both near-term algorithmic benchmarks and a long-term perspective can be found in digital quantum simulation, we specifically discuss the fermionic fast Fourier transform and the simulation of Fermi-Hubbard models. The latter is explicitly discussed in the context of quantum error correction and a partially fault-tolerant realization. By providing detailed resource estimates and identifying scaling bottlenecks on each level, our work offers a quantitative perspective on EO-based quantum computing and will inform future hardware design choices.

item.title: Matrix Holography on an Optical Lattice
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Constructs bosonic four-body matrix-quantum-mechanics potentials via Floquet-engineered oscillating two-body spin interactions with a constant number of unitaries per cycle. Control-frequency bandwidth scales as 𝒪(N3) with matrix size N, reaching non-perturbative couplings λ∼𝒪(1) at driving frequencies ω∼𝒪(MHz).

Grade 0.403 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “analog quantum simulation of lattice models on cold atoms or superconducting ar…” · Robin Löwenberg, Julian Sonner

Figure

Ground-state energy convergence as a function of spin size j comparing the large-spin model against the truncated SU(2)×SO(2) bosonic matrix model with λ=2 and cutoff Λ=6. Relative error is 0.5% at j=3 and drops to 0.007%.

Asks

Can four-body potentials of bosonic matrix quantum mechanics be simulated on an analog optical-lattice platform without the deep circuits of digital implementations?

But

Requires non-spin-conserving spin-spin interactions and large-spin ferromagnetic regime (m∼j). Bosonic Hilbert space must be truncated.

Tools

Holstein-Primakoff transformation · Floquet engineering · Magnus expansion · James' effective Hamiltonian method · optical lattice of atomic ensembles

Abstract

We propose an analog quantum-simulation protocol based on a lattice of atomic ensembles and time-averaged Floquet dynamics to construct the four-body potentials that typically appear in bosonic BFSS-like matrix quantum mechanics. In contrast to gate-based digital implementations requiring deep circuits, our approach generates the target model through a fixed set of control stages per Floquet cycle, keeping the number of consecutive unitaries constant with respect to the matrix size N. The principal scaling cost in our construction is given by the frequency range required to control the growing lattice. We show that this cost grows at most as O(N³), giving a polynomial scaling route to large-N, attractive to experimental implementation. Additionally, we demonstrate that the coupling parameter can be tuned beyond O(1), enabling the simulation of strong-coupling physics necessary for holographic phases.

item.title: Wavelength-Uniform Quantum Algorithms for Quantum Dynamics
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Constructed an end-to-end quantum algorithm for the von Neumann equation with polynomial complexity in dimension d and resource bounds containing no negative powers of the semiclassical parameter ε. Evaluated physical observables uniformly across ε∈[10−4,1] with observable error Eobs≤6.8126×10−7 under fixed grid parameters.

Grade 0.403 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Shi Jin, Chuwen Ma

Figure

Observable error Eobs as a function of grid refinement parameters and across nine values of ε from 10−4 to 1, demonstrating ε-uniform convergence below the 10−5 tolerance with fixed (M,K,Q)=(256,36,16).

Asks

How can quantum dynamics in the semiclassical regime ε≪1 be simulated on a quantum computer without spatial mesh and query constraints scaling inversely with ε?

Before

Standard spatial spectral methods and wave-function representations require spatial mesh h=O(ε) and O(ε−d) spatial unknowns due to the Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem; Gaussian wave-packet methods require h=O(ε) and cost O(ε−d/2) per step.

But

Applies to smooth physical observables (pairing with Lx,y2 windows) rather than full density matrix state reconstruction; requires uniform regularity of the density operator in Weyl variables.

Tools

Weyl variables · Hermite-Galerkin projection · Quantum Singular Value Transformation (QSVT) · Linear Combination of Unitaries (LCU) · Qubitized Hamiltonian simulation

Abstract

One of the main challenges in quantum simulation is the prohibitive cost of computing its solutions in the semi-classical regime, in which the de Broglie wavelength is small compared with the characteristic length scale and the solution is highly oscillatory. This difficulty is overcome by using the Weyl variable, under which the solution is not oscillatory. Furthermore, we use the exact Hermite moments and quantum singular value transformation to treat the polynomial and Fourier components of the potential, resulting in a quantum algorithm efficient for all ranges of wavelengths. Specifically, it has a polynomial complexity in spatial dimension, and discretization and query bounds without negative powers of possibly small wavelength, thus enabling it to capture the correct physical observables even if the spatial grid does not resolve the frequency, hence defying the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem.

item.title: A Platform-aware Compilation Framework for Fault-tolerant Quantum Computation
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Unified compilation pipeline produces hardware-tailored FTQC resource estimates across three connectivity classes, showing that small-molecule chemistry (trimethylenemethane) requires ∼104 physical qubits with runtimes of 102 ms (photonic, superconducting) to 105 ms (neutral atoms).

Grade 0.402 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Srushti Patil, Susan X. Chen, Andreas Juul Bay-Smidt, Stefan Alaric Schäffer, Peter Krogstrup, Stefano Paesani, Gemma C. Solomon

Figure

Physical qubit count versus runtime for the Stat-QPE-gap TMM benchmark across multiple compiler-hardware architectures at error rates p=10−3 and p=10−4.

Asks

How can quantum circuits and fault-tolerant architectures be compiled to enable accurate, platform-aware end-to-end resource estimation across distinct physical hardware modalities?

But

Trotterized phase estimation and simulation; surface-code Clifford + T gate model; physical error rates p=10−3 and p=10−4.

Tools

Transversal active volume (t-AV) architecture · ZX-diagram logical blocks · Pauli product rotation compiler · Lattice surgery · Surface code

Abstract

The compilation of an algorithm can vary significantly with the choice of physical hardware platform and error correction model. Yet, current compilation frameworks typically commit to a single architecture-hardware configuration, making it difficult to assess resource estimates across platforms. We present a platform-aware compilation framework that re-compiles a quantum circuit into a hardware-compatible instruction set as well as fault-tolerant operations and provides end-to-end resource estimates in terms of physical-qubit count, time-to-solution, and classical processing time. We benchmark the framework by obtaining end-to-end resource estimates for different compilers, each tailored to the functionalities of specific hardware modalities: connectivity, clock speed, and noise model. As part of this framework, we introduce a transversal active volume (t-AV) compilation architecture designed for the efficient execution of fault-tolerant operations in platforms supporting long-range logical connectivity. We benchmark the framework for Hamiltonian simulation of the 2D Fermi Hubbard model as well as for eigenenergy estimation of a small molecule (trimethylenemethane) as a candidate for early fault-tolerant demonstration of quantum chemistry. For the latter, we show that end-to-end quantum simulations can be achieved with ∼10⁴ physical qubits and runtimes ranging from 10² ms (photonics, superconducting) to 10⁵ ms (neutral atoms).

item.title: Efficient Quantum Circuits for Electronic Hamiltonian Simulation without Pauli Expansion
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Diagonalizing ladder-string-pair (Lasp) operators directly avoids Pauli expansion for electronic Hamiltonian simulation, reducing CX-gate count from 36 to 12 in a 4-index triad and from O(n2) to O(n) across O(n) ordered triads without introducing Trotter error at the triad level.

Grade 0.370 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Tamiya Onodera, Takeshi Sato

Figure

High-level quantum circuits for time evolution of a fermionic triad before and after CX cancellation, showing reduction from 36 CX gates to 12 CX gates alongside three C3RZ gates.

Asks

How can electronic Hamiltonian simulation circuits be constructed and optimized directly from fermionic ladder operators without Pauli expansion?

Before

Standard simulation expands fermionic ladder products into Pauli strings, producing 16 Pauli strings per two-body Lasp operator and O(n2) CX scaling.

But

Theoretical circuit construction and gate-count optimization. Systematic optimization for global triad ordering and composition across all index groups left for future work.

Tools

ladder-string-pair (Lasp) diagonalization · Jordan–Wigner transformation · GHZ state preparation circuits · parity encoding circuits · multi-controlled Z rotations (C3RZ/C4RZ)

Abstract

Electronic Hamiltonian simulation is commonly formulated by mapping fermionic operators to qubit operators and subsequently expanding the resulting ladder-operator products into Pauli strings. While general, this procedure obscures the higher-level fermionic structure and can hide opportunities for circuit optimization. Building on ladder-string-pair (Lasp) diagonalization originally developed for Hamiltonian simulation of partial differential equations, we construct time-evolution circuits for the second-quantized electronic Hamiltonian without performing a Pauli expansion. For the most general case of complex-valued coefficients, we present a time-evolution circuit for a two-body fermionic Lasp operator that corresponds to 16 Pauli strings in the Pauli-expansion approach but does not suffer from Trotter error at this stage. Expanding the optimization scope from a single operator to a triad of three fermionic Lasp operators sharing the same four spin-orbital indices enables systematic cancellation of CX gates, reducing the CX-gate count from 36 to 12 in the example considered, still without introducing Trotter error at this stage. For n spin orbitals, further expanding the optimization scope to a sequence of O(n) suitably ordered triads enables a cascade of CX-gate reductions across triad boundaries, reducing the CX-gate count from O(n²) to O(n). The Lasp-based approach also naturally accommodates controlled time evolution and yields further optimizations for real-valued Hamiltonians. These results demonstrate that the Lasp-based approach enables more efficient time-evolution circuits by preserving high-level circuit structures and thereby expanding the scope of optimization, providing a systematic route toward more efficient electronic Hamiltonian simulation.

item.title: Benchmarking dynamical-structure-factor protocols in programmable neutral-atom geometries
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Emulation of Raman-spectroscopy dynamical structure factor protocol on neutral-atom quantum processors successfully reconstructs magnon excitation dispersions for 1D and 2D transverse-field Ising models with N up to 36 atoms, remaining robust under realistic laser noise and positional disorder.

Grade 0.366 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Matteo Grotti, Sergi Julià-Farré, Elisa Ercolessi, Alexandre Dauphin

Figure

Reconstructed dynamical structure factor Szz(kx,ky=π,ω) plotted against momentum kx (horizontal axis) and frequency ω/hx (vertical axis) for 2D square lattices (4×4 with periodic boundaries, 6×6 with open boundaries) at J/hx=0.1 and 0.2.

Asks

Can programmable neutral-atom quantum processors accurately measure dynamical structure factors in 1D dimerized and 2D non-integrable transverse-field Ising models under realistic experimental noise?

But

Numerical emulation rather than physical hardware. Assumes paramagnetic regime hx/J≫1; classical validation accuracy degrades near quantum phase transition (J/hx=0.4). Noise averaging performed over 50 trajectories before Fourier transformation.

Tools

Pulser neutral-atom emulator · Matrix product states (emu-mps) · State-vector emulation (emu-sv) · Rydberg tweezer Hamiltonian dynamics

Abstract

The dynamical structure factor is a central observable in condensed-matter physics, providing direct insight into the excitation spectrum and dynamical response of quantum materials. While it is traditionally accessed in real materials through inelastic neutron scattering, recent works have shown that analogous information can be extracted in quantum simulators using suitable dynamical protocols. So far, these approaches have been demonstrated mainly in paradigmatic integrable one-dimensional models. In this work, we use numerical emulations of a neutral-atom quantum processing unit to assess the feasibility of measuring the dynamical structure factor in a broader class of Ising-like spin systems. Beyond the standard one-dimensional transverse-field Ising chain, we benchmark the protocol in chains with dimerized interactions and in the two-dimensional transverse-field Ising model, where spectral properties are difficult to access with classical numerical methods at large scales. We further analyze the robustness of the protocol under realistic experimental conditions, including finite simulation times, pulse modulation, positional disorder, and laser noise. Our results show that neutral-atom quantum simulators can provide a practical route to probing dynamical response functions in regimes where classical simulations become increasingly demanding, paving the way toward experimental implementation.

item.title: From Bits to Qubits: The Theory and Practice of Quantum Data Encoding
item.description:
Worth a look review — Surveys quantum data encoding methods across state preparation, unitary synthesis, QRAM, and block-encoding, synthesizing circuit size, depth, and fault-tolerant gate counts.

Grade 0.363 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Xiao-Ming Zhang, Arthur G. Rattew, Bujiao Wu, Georgios Styliaris, Xiaoming Sun, Bálint Koczor, Xiao Yuan

Figure

Three core access models mapping classical vectors and matrices to quantum operations: quantum state preparation, QRAM, and block-encoding.

Asks

How can deterministic classical data be compiled into quantum representations under minimal circuit depth, gate counts, and non-Clifford resources?

But

Restricted to deterministic, fully known classical data in the standard qubit circuit model with all-to-all or binary-tree connectivity; excludes sampled distributions and continuous variables.

Tools

uniformly controlled rotations (UCR) · Schmidt decomposition · QRAM bucket-brigade architecture · linear combination of unitaries (LCU) · block-encoding

Abstract

Encoding classical data into quantum systems is a foundational step in the execution of nearly all quantum algorithms, and a critical bottleneck in realizing practical quantum advantage. This review provides a comprehensive account of the concepts, algorithms, and practical considerations associated with quantum data encoding. We trace the development from its early conceptual foundations to recent advances, considering commonly used access models, such as quantum state preparation, unitary synthesis, QRAM and block encoding. We survey the circuit size, depth, space-time tradeoffs, as well as non-Clifford resources required for fault-tolerant implementation. We also discuss the roles of different access models in quantum algorithms. Special attention is given to structured data, such as sparse data, Boolean functions and data represented by tensor networks. This review bridges theory and applications, serving both as a pedagogical guide for newcomers and as a reference for active researchers. We also highlight the pivotal role of quantum data encoding in quantum computing and provide insights into future directions that will enable quantum advantage.
